what_its_for: Hydrochlorothiazide is a 'water pill' (diuretic) that helps your kidneys remove extra salt and water from your body through your urine. It is used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) and swelling (edema) caused by heart failure, kidney problems, or liver disease. Lowering high blood pressure helps prevent strokes, heart attacks, and kidney problems.
how_to_take: Take this medicine by mouth, with or without food. If it upsets your stomach, try taking it with food or milk. Take it early in the morning so that having to urinate more often does not disturb your sleep at night. Swallow the tablet or capsule whole with a full glass of water. Try to take it at the same time every day to help you remember.
dosing: The usual starting dose for adults is 12.5 mg to 25 mg once a day. Your doctor may increase your dose up to 50 mg per day depending on how your body responds. For children, the dose is based on body weight and is decided by the doctor. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions — do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is still the same day. If it is already the next day or almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do NOT take two doses at the same time to make up for the one you missed. Missing an occasional dose is not usually dangerous, but try to be consistent.
storage: Store at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, direct light, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about the best way to dispose of it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking this medicine because it can increase the blood pressure-lowering effect and make you feel dizzy or faint. Avoid standing up too quickly from sitting or lying down, as this can cause dizziness. Limit exposure to sunlight and tanning beds — this drug can make your skin more sensitive to the sun, so use sunscreen and wear protective clothing. Avoid taking extra doses of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) or naproxen (Aleve) without talking to your doctor, as they can reduce how well this medicine works. Be careful with salt substitutes or potassium supplements unless your doctor tells you to use them.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience: signs of low potassium such as muscle weakness, cramps, or an irregular heartbeat; signs of dehydration such as extreme thirst, dry mouth, little or no urination, or feeling very dizzy; signs of a severe allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing; signs of high blood sugar such as increased thirst and frequent urination; eye pain or sudden vision changes; yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice); unusual bleeding or bruising; or severe nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
when_it_works: For high blood pressure, you may start to see your blood pressure lowering within a few days, but it can take 3 to 4 weeks to get the full benefit. For swelling (edema), you will likely notice increased urination and reduced swelling within a few hours of your first dose. Keep taking this medicine even if you feel well — high blood pressure often has no symptoms, and stopping too soon can be harmful.
special_populations: Older adults: You may be more sensitive to the effects of this medicine, especially dizziness and low blood pressure. Be extra careful when standing up to avoid falls. Pregnancy: This medicine is generally not recommended during pregnancy, especially in the second and third trimesters. Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant. Breastfeeding: Small amounts of this medicine can pass into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Kidney or liver disease: Your doctor may need to adjust your dose or monitor you more closely. Diabetes: This medicine may raise blood sugar levels, so your doctor may need to adjust your diabetes medicines. Always tell all your doctors and your pharmacist about every medicine, vitamin, and supplement you take.
